claims.statement: The OAuth Server-to-Server credential generates access tokens with the OAuth 2.0 client_credentials grant, using the credential's client_id and client_secret (with scopes) in a token request; the client_secret must be used only on a secure backend server.

sources.supports: OAuth Server-to-Server credential relies on the client_credentials grant; a single HTTP request with client_id, client_secret and scopes generates a token; the logic must run on a secure backend server to prevent malicious actors from accessing secrets.

Fetching access tokens: client_id (mandatory, the Client ID from the Developer Console) and client_secret (mandatory, the value of client secret obtained from the Developer Console) are request parameters.

claims.statement: A credential can hold up to 2 client secrets; secrets can be added, listed (the list returns only a uuid and metadata, never the secret value) and deleted through the Developer Console UI or the I/O Management API; the add response returns the new client_secret once, and it is otherwise visible only in the Developer Console UI.

sources.supports: You can add up to 2 client secrets; no client_secret values are returned by the list API; the add response contains the client_secret, which will never be returned in plain text by any other API response.
sources.locator: sections "List all client secrets" and "Add client secret to credential"

sources.supports: Secrets can be rotated through the Dev Console UI and programmatically; a deleted client secret cannot be restored.

claims.statement: For the OAuth Server-to-Server credential the client secret is sent to the token endpoint as the request parameter client_secret, together with client_id, grant_type=client_credentials and scope, in an application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST body or as query parameters; the page recommends the body for sensitive data because query parameters may be logged by app servers.

sources.supports: client_secret is a mandatory parameter described as the value of client secret obtained from the Developer Console; parameters can be sent in the body or as query parameters, and passing parameters in the body is recommended for sensitive data.
sources.locator: section "Fetching access tokens", Parameters table and cURL request

sources.supports: The cURL example posts client_id, client_secret, grant_type=client_credentials and scope as a form-encoded body to the token endpoint, with client_id and client_secret shown as {CLIENT_ID} and {CLIENT_SECRET} placeholders.

claims.statement: The documentation shows the client secret only as a placeholder: {CLIENT_SECRET} in request examples and a run of X characters in the add-secret sample response; the sample list response shows only secret uuid values and metadata, never a secret value. No page read states a prefix, alphabet, length or checksum for the secret.

sources.supports: Sample responses for adding a client secret (client_secret shown as a run of X characters) and listing client secrets (uuid and metadata only); the page states no format for the value.
sources.locator: sections "Add client secret to credential" and "List all client secrets", Sample Response

sources.supports: Request examples use {CLIENT_SECRET} placeholders; the page states no format for the value.

claims.statement: Two open-source scanner rule artifacts from different maintainers (Gitleaks, Praetorian's Nosey Parker) both treat a string beginning with the literal prefix "p8e-" as an Adobe client secret. Neither artifact says which Adobe credential type the secret belongs to, neither cites an Adobe page that states the prefix, and neither is a provider statement. This claim covers the prefix only and is not attributed to this family (see the open question on subtype attribution).

sources.supports: Rule adobe-client-secret is described as an Adobe Client Secret and uses the regular expression fragment p8e- followed by a body, with the keyword p8e-.
sources.locator: cmd/generate/config/rules/adobe.go lines 24-31 at the pinned commit

sources.supports: Rule np.adobe.1 "Adobe OAuth Client Secret" matches p8e- followed by a body, with Adobe Developer Console authentication pages as references.

claims.statement: Each of the same two rule artifacts states a body of 32 characters after the "p8e-" prefix. The length is as each rule states it; whether it holds for every issued secret, and whether the prefix applies to every issued secret, is not established.

sources.supports: The expression is p8e-(?i)[a-z0-9]{32}: a 32-character body.
sources.locator: cmd/generate/config/rules/adobe.go line 29 at the pinned commit

sources.supports: The pattern is p8e-[a-z0-9-]{32}: a 32-character body.

claims.statement: The two rule artifacts differ on the body alphabet: one admits letters and digits (its case-insensitive flag follows the literal prefix), the other admits letters, digits and hyphen under a global case-insensitive flag. Whether an issued secret body can contain a hyphen is unresolved.

sources.locator: cmd/generate/config/rules/adobe.go line 29 at the pinned commit

sources.supports: Body class [a-z0-9-] under a global (?i) flag.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Revision 2 supersedes revision 1, which is left unchanged. Changes: structure.prefixes ["p8e-"] is removed because no source attributes the p8e- prefix to this credential type (revision 1 itself recorded that neither rule names a type); the combined prefix, length and alphabet claim is split into three (the prefix claim keeps its id); request-parameter and placeholder claims are added; the two provider-documented claims are carried over verbatim and re-read on 2026-10-05.

openQuestions.question: No Adobe page read on 2026-10-05 states a prefix, alphabet, length or checksum for the client secret; the pages show only placeholders. Settled by an Adobe statement of the secret format, or by an issued sample under a maintainer's authority (issuance-gated).

Whether a p8e- secret is an OAuth Server-to-Server, OAuth Web App or Enterprise Web App client secret, or any of them, is not established: the rule artifacts name no type and the provider pages read do not mention the prefix. Settled by an Adobe statement that ties the prefix to a credential type, or an Adobe-published example of a secret of a named type.

Whether the two rules were written independently is not shown: neither states how its prefix was derived. The Nosey Parker rule lists three Adobe documentation URLs as references; on 2026-10-05 two were readable and neither contained the prefix, and one (the OAuthIntegration page under the authentication guide) returned HTTP 404. Settled by the rules' authors stating their basis, or by an Adobe page stating the prefix.

Whether every issued client secret begins with p8e-, including secrets added later through the I/O Management API or the Developer Console and secrets of earlier eras, is not stated. Settled by an Adobe statement or by issuance-gated observation.

The list-secrets sample response shows an example client_id (a 32-character lowercase hexadecimal value) but the pages give no rule for it. The client ID is a public identifier (sent as the x-api-key header) and must not be treated as the secret; client ID and secret are distinguishable by documented role, not by a documented shape.

Lead, not recorded as a claim: another open-source scanner's Adobe detector looks for a 32-character lowercase alphanumeric value near the word adobe and a 12-character identifier; it concerns an API key and identifier, not this secret, and is not corroboration of the claims above.
